gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a named reviewer has bench-tested any long-cord strip: TechGearLab's surge-protector test (Chris McNamara and Ian Nicholson; page updated 2023-12-19) included the 15 ft CRST 10-Outlet Heavy Duty, gave it the top cord score (9.0, highest of the 10 models), found every tested cord was at least 14 AWG, and reported that all units held around 120 V under heavy load.
standout_why: I compared against rottenwifi.com (2026-09-30). It says outright that its figures are 'not a fresh head-to-head laboratory test' and gives only maker or listing ratings, such as 500 V UL 1449 for the Belkin BE112234-10 and Tripp Lite TLP606B. The retailer and maker pages ChatGPT got (Home Depot, Walmart DEWENWILS, Office Depot, Newegg, Eaton, CRST) are spec listings with no measurements. I couldn't read gearlark.com because of an SSL certificate error. Technically the TechGearLab data is new to this answer, but it's thin. It dates from 2023, its voltage result covers the whole test group rather than each model, and it tested none of the four products ChatGPT showed. It adds little, so I scored it 1, not 2.
decides: It doesn't decide the pick. None of the strips ChatGPT showed (GoGreen 15 ft, TESSAN 15 ft and 25 ft, Tripp Lite PS725B) has a named measurement I could find. The only long-cord strip a named reviewer tested is the CRST 10-outlet 15 ft. Against ChatGPT's picks, that supports at most a note like 'the only 15 ft strip with hands-on testing is the CRST'. The page should not claim any measured advantage for one strip over another.

findings.label: TechGearLab cord-length score
findings.value: 9.0 / 10 (highest of the 10 models tested; overall score 76)
findings.source_title: Best Surge Protectors and Power Strips (TechGearLab)
findings.note: Article updated 2023-12-19 by Chris McNamara with Ian Nicholson. Cord length is weighted 10% of the total score, and the article doesn't explain how it was scored. TechGearLab: the '15-foot heavy-duty power cord ... often allowed us to bypass using an extension cord.' The 2800 J rating it quotes is CRST's own figure, not a measurement.

findings.label: TechGearLab voltage under load, all 10 tested strips
findings.value: around 120 V held 'even with a lot of higher-drawing devices plugged in'
findings.source_title: Best Surge Protectors and Power Strips (TechGearLab)
findings.note: Tested with multimeters, non-contact voltage testers and outlet testers. A photo caption shows Ian Nicholson 'measuring how much electricity is lost while 4 amps are being pulled out'. No figure is given per model, and the meter and load used for the 120 V result aren't named. This is not a surge-injection or let-through test.

findings.label: TechGearLab cord gauge across tested strips
findings.value: at least 14 AWG on every model tested (cords from 2 ft to 15 ft)
findings.source_title: Best Surge Protectors and Power Strips (TechGearLab)
findings.note: TechGearLab: 'All of the models we tested had at least a 14 AWG (gauge) cord.' Of the tested models, only the CRST had a cord of 10 ft or more.

findings.label: Measurement status of the rival long-cord article
findings.value: no independent measurements ('not a fresh head-to-head laboratory test')
findings.source_title: Best Corded Surge Protectors: Belkin BE112234-10 vs. TLP606B (RottenWiFi, 2026-09-30)
findings.note: Its only let-through or clamping figures are maker-stated UL 1449 ratings: 500 V for the Belkin BE112234-10 and 500 V for the Tripp Lite TLP606B. Neither strip's cord is longer than 10 ft.
